title: Standing out from the crowd
caption: The globular cluster NGC 6642, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 6642 · constellation Sagittarius · about 25000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This Hubble view looks into the core of NGC 6642, a globular cluster in our own galaxy whose center is packed so tightly with stars that it is a hard target for most telescopes. A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical swarm of stars held together by gravity.

That crowding cuts both ways. Because the stars in such a cluster share a similar age, together they preserve clues to the chemical makeup of the Milky Way early in its history. But the same density makes individual stars near the core hard to pick apart. NGC 6642 has a further problem. It sits in a very central part of our galaxy, so any picture of it also catches many 'field stars' that are not part of the cluster at all.

Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys can identify and remove those interlopers and resolve the crowded core in unprecedented detail. Studies with it have turned up many 'blue stragglers', stars that seem to age more slowly than their neighbors, and shown that the cluster is short of low-mass stars.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (1.62 x 1.67 arcminutes) and distance (25000 light years), the frame spans roughly 12 × 12 light-years. Its light set out about 25,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and infrared exposures from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The infrared exposure records light the eye cannot see, and Hubble's sharp view separates stars in a core that most telescopes cannot resolve.

explore: The cluster lies about 25,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius. The picture combines visible and infrared exposures from the Advanced Camera for Surveys' Wide Field Channel and covers a patch of sky roughly 1.6 arcminutes on each side.
alt: A crowded field of stars thickening toward the dense core of the globular cluster NGC 6642.
